Lessons.Title: Division With and Without Remainders
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 goal: Find whole-number quotients and remainders for up to four-digit dividends divided by one-digit divisors using partial quotients.
Warm-up: 100=33×3+1, 200=66×3+2, 300=100×3; identify the pattern of remainders of hundreds divided by three.
Activity 1: Analyze Jada's 389÷7: subtract 280, then 49, then 56; 4 remains and partial quotients 40+7+8=55. Divide 702÷3=234 without a remainder.

Activity 2: Andre and Elena make recording mistakes for 2316÷5. Predict remainder from the final digit; a valid calculation produces quotient 463, remainder 1. Students explain why and correct the original student algorithms with teacher.
Activity 3: Complete at least two partial-quotient approaches to 3294÷3. Parts 3000,270,24 give partial quotients 1000,90,8; the quotient is 1098. Or 3300÷3−6÷3=1098.
First-party Edulytics Cool-down (not the source gated item): 947÷4=236 remainder 3, checked by 4×236+3=947.

KeyConcepts.Title: Valid remainder
KeyConcepts.Definition: Whole units left over after forming all complete divisor-sized groups.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial-quotient subtraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtract a divisible chunk and record how many groups that chunk contains.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every subtraction equals divisor×partial quotient; add partial quotients.

KeyConcepts.Title: Error checking
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use estimation, multiples and the quotient-remainder identity to detect recorded mistakes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A purported subtraction of 2000 for quotient 40 at divisor 5 is wrong because 5×40=200.
KeyConcepts.Example: 2316=5×463+1; 463 is reasonable and 103 is far too small.

WorkedExamples.Title: Jada's stack: 389 ÷ 7
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain the partial quotients and remainder in Jada's calculation.
WorkedExamples.Method: Match every subtracted multiple of 7 to its partial quotient.
Steps: Subtract 7×7=49 to leave 60, then 7×8=56 to leave 4.
Add 40+7+8=55 and identify 4 as a remainder smaller than 7.

WorkedExamples.Title: 702 ÷ 3 with no remainder
WorkedExamples.Question: Use partial quotients to divide 702 into three equal groups.
WorkedExamples.Method: Subtract large multiples of 3 and finish at zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Andre and Elena: 2316 ÷ 5
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain the expected remainder and show a correct record to check their work.
WorkedExamples.Method: Predict divisibility, then subtract matched partial products.
Steps: A number ending in 6 is not divisible by 5; it must leave a remainder.

WorkedExamples.Title: Incomplete records: 3294 ÷ 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Complete two different ways to divide 3294 by 3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Partial quotients or a nearby multiple correction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rounding a leftover up to a complete group.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Four leftover items cannot make a seven-item group.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtracting 2000 but recording a partial quotient of 40 at divisor 5.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Five times forty is two hundred, not two thousand.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting a remainder greater than or equal to the divisor.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One or more additional complete groups could still be made.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Continue dividing until the remainder is smaller than the divisor.

SummaryPoints: Record each subtracted divisible chunk and the matching partial quotient.
Remainder may be zero or positive, but always less than the divisor.
Use dividend=divisor×quotient+remainder to check source answers and detect errors.
Teacher checks the student-written algorithm and critiques, which numeric Practice alone does not grade.
